\[
\|f-g\|_{L_2(\mu)}>\varepsilon
\qquad\text{for all distinct } f,g\in F.
\]
If
\[
n\ge C\varepsilon^{-4}\log |F|,
\]
then, with probability at least \(0.99\), the empirical measure \(\mu_n\) satisfies
\[
\|f-g\|_{L_2(\mu_n)}>\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
\qquad\text{for all distinct } f,g\in F.
\]

By the definition of the empirical measure (see Section 8.2.3), \(\|f-g\|_{L_2(\mu_n)}\) is the same as in (8.31), but with the population average replaced by the sample average:

\tag{8.32}
\]
where \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are i.i.d. copies of \(X\).

**Theorem 7.2.2 (Slepian inequality).** Let \((X_t)_{t\in T}\) and \((Y_t)_{t\in T}\) be two mean-zero Gaussian processes. Assume that, for all \(t,s\in T\),
\[
\mathbb{E}X_t^2=\mathbb{E}Y_t^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb{E}(X_t-X_s)^2\le \mathbb{E}(Y_t-Y_s)^2. \tag{7.3}
\]
Then \(\sup_{t\in T}X_t\) is stochastically dominated by \(\sup_{t\in T}Y_t\): for every \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\left\{\sup_{t\in T}X_t\ge\tau\right\}
\le
\mathbb{P}\left\{\sup_{t\in T}Y_t\ge\tau\right\}. \tag{7.4}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb{E}\sup_{t\in T}X_t\le \mathbb{E}\sup_{t\in T}Y_t. \tag{7.5}
\]
